relevance_reason: The abstract reports PRPH2 mutations in French families with autosomal dominant RP. It gives prevalence, a functional study of the novel recurrent p.Leu254Gln variant and clinical features, all of which are relevant to the PRPH2-related RP7 entry.

findings.statement: Manes et al. (2015) screened PRPH2 by Sanger sequencing in 310 French families with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa. They identified 15 mutations (6 novel and 9 previously reported) in 32 families, a prevalence of 10.3%. This was higher than previously reported (0 to 8%) and made PRPH2 the second most frequent adRP gene after RHO in their series.
quotes: PRPH2 was screened by Sanger sequencing in a cohort of 310 French families with adRP.
We identified 15 mutations, including 6 novel and 9 previously reported changes in 32 families, accounting for a prevalence of 10.3% in this adRP population.
This makes PRPH2 the second most frequent adRP gene after RHO in our series.

findings.statement: Manes et al. (2015) identified a novel recurrent p.Leu254Gln mutation in PRPH2 in French families with autosomal dominant RP. Peripherin-2 carrying this mutation was produced in yeast and analyzed by Western blot. The mutant protein aggregated, which the authors suggested indicates abnormal folding.
quotes: We showed that a new recurrent p.Leu254Gln mutation leads to protein aggregation, suggesting abnormal folding.
Peripherin-2 protein was produced in yeast and analyzed by Western blot.

findings.statement: Manes et al. (2015) found that disease severity was moderate in patients with adRP and PRPH2 mutations. Visual acuity was 1 to 0.5 in 78% of eyes, and 52% of eyes retained more than 50% of the visual field. Some patients characteristically had vitelliform deposits or macular involvement. Within some families, certain members had pericentral RP or macular dystrophy while others had widespread RP. The authors concluded that PRPH2 mutations cause highly variable phenotypes and moderate forms of adRP, including mild cases that could be underdiagnosed.
quotes: The clinical severity of the disease in examined patients was moderate with 78% of the eyes having 1-0.5 of visual acuity and 52% of the eyes retaining more than 50% of the visual field.

Some patients characteristically showed vitelliform deposits or macular involvement. In some families, pericentral RP or macular dystrophy were found in family members while widespread RP was present in other members of the same families.
PRPH2 mutations cause highly variable phenotypes and moderate forms of adRP, including mild cases, which could be underdiagnosed.

relevance_reason: This targeted NGS study of patients with LCA or juvenile RP found homozygous PRPH2 mutations, including p.L185P (the PRPH2 allele in digenic RP7), causing severe early-onset retinal dystrophy. Heterozygous carriers had macular pattern dystrophy. This adds allelic and phenotypic evidence for the RP7 gene.

findings.statement: Wang et al. (2013) described 3 unrelated patients (1318, 3256, and 741) homozygous for PRPH2 missense mutations. Two had LCA and one had juvenile RP. All had visual impairment within the first year of life, nondetectable or reduced ERGs, and a very similar maculopathy in the fundus. The 2 LCA patients also had nystagmus. Fundus findings included a multilobulated central atrophic maculopathy, vessel narrowing, peripheral pigment deposits or diffuse retinal dystrophy, and optic disc pallor in 1 patient.
quotes: All the patients with homozygous mutations in PRPH2 exhibited LCA or juvenile RP phenotypes, including visual impairment within the first year of life, nystagmus in the two LCA patients (1318 and 3256), non-detectable or reduced ERGs, and a very similar form of maculopathies in the fundus

Fundus photographs of patient 3256 show pigment deposits both peripherally and in the macular region, extensive disease with choroidal sclerosis, vessel narrowing, and optic disc pallor; a central extensive atrophic maculopathy is seen in C and D.
Fundus photograph of patient 741 shows the obvious diffuse retinal dystrophy with retinal vessel narrowing, retinal pigment epithelium mottling and loss, and a multilobulated maculopathy.

phenotypes.text: visual impairment within first year of life

findings.statement: Wang et al. (2013) used targeted NGS of 163 retinal disease genes to study patients with LCA or juvenile RP. In LCA patient 3256, they found a homozygous c.554T>C (p.L185P) missense mutation in PRPH2. They noted that this mutation had previously been reported to cause digenic RP together with a ROM1 null mutation. They then sequenced PRPH2 in 135 more unsolved patients and found the same homozygous p.L185P mutation in juvenile RP patient 741, whose parents were both heterozygous. The mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
quotes: the p.L185P mutation, together with a null mutation in ROM1, has been reported to cause digenic RP
we sequenced PRPH2 in another 135 unsolved LCA or juvenile RP patients and found the same homozygous missense mutation p.L185P in PRPH2 in a third juvenile RP patient, 741.
The c.554T>C mutation is homozygous in patient 741 and heterozygous in both parents.

findings.statement: Wang et al. (2013) found a homozygous c.637T>C (p.C213R) missense mutation in PRPH2 in LCA patient 1318. This mutation had previously been associated with autosomal dominant pattern dystrophy. The patient's mother and son were heterozygous carriers, and an unaffected brother was homozygous wild-type.
quotes: Each patient carried a reported homozygous missense mutation in gene PRPH2: c.637T>C (p.C213R) and c.554T>C (p.L185P), respectively (table 7).
The c.637T>C mutation is homozygous in patient 1318, heterozygous in both parents and the son, and homozygous wild-type in the brother.

findings.statement: Wang et al. (2013) found that relatives heterozygous for PRPH2 mutations had no symptoms but showed detectable macular pattern dystrophy. The 56-year-old heterozygous father of patient 741 (p.L185P) had macular pattern dystrophy with essentially normal visual acuity. The 57-year-old mother of patient 1318 (p.C213R) had a butterfly-shaped macular pattern dystrophy with 20/20 acuity. The authors suggested that the severe early-onset disease in homozygotes reflects a dose-dependent effect, consistent with rds mouse models. They also suggested that heterozygous p.L185P carriers, previously reported as asymptomatic in digenic RP families, may have a subclinical phenotype.
quotes: the 56-year-old father of patient 741 had macular pattern dystrophy and clear-cut foveal changes, but his visual acuity was essentially normal in both eyes
At 57 years of age, the mother was asymptomatic with 20/20 visual acuity but had a florid butterfly-shaped macular pattern dystrophy and a number of other retinal flecks upon examination
individuals harbouring the heterozygous p.L185P mutation should be expected to exhibit a subclinical phenotype

relevance_reason: Reports an RDS (peripherin) codon 118/119 cysteine deletion in a family with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa, which directly supports RDS-associated RP (RP7); also contrasts it with RDS mutations causing macular dystrophy.

findings.statement: Wells et al. (1993) screened the RDS gene, which encodes the photoreceptor glycoprotein peripherin, in families with autosomal dominant retinal dystrophies. In one family with retinitis pigmentosa, they found a deletion of a cysteine at codon 118/119 of RDS.
quotes: Mutations in the RDS gene, which encodes the photoreceptor glycoprotein peripherin, have been sought in families with autosomal dominant retinal dystrophies.
A cysteine deletion at codon 118/119 is associated with retinitis pigmentosa in one.

findings.statement: Wells et al. (1993) found that, in contrast to the RP-associated codon 118/119 cysteine deletion, three families with similar macular dystrophy had RDS mutations at codon 172 (arg172-to-trp in two families and arg172-to-gln in one), and a family with adult vitelliform macular dystrophy had a stop codon at codon 258. They concluded that both retinitis pigmentosa and macular dystrophies are caused by RDS mutations and that the functional significance of certain amino acids in peripherin-RDS may differ in cones and rods.
quotes: Three families with similar macular dystrophy have mutations at codon 172, arginine being substituted by tryptophan in two and by glutamine in one.
A stop sequence at codon 258 exists in a family with adult vitelliform macular dystrophy.
both retinitis pigmentosa and macular dystrophies are caused by mutations in RDS and that the functional significance of certain amino-acids in peripherin-RDS may be different in cones and rods

relevance_reason: The paper reports a family with a peripherin/RDS (PRPH2) codon 153/154 deletion causing retinitis pigmentosa and other phenotypes. This is direct evidence for the PRPH2-related RP7 phenotype.

findings.statement: Weleber et al. (1993) described a family in which a 75-year-old woman, her two daughters (aged 44 and 50 years) and her 49-year-old son showed three different phenotypes. The mother presented at age 63 years with adult-onset retinitis pigmentosa and a profoundly abnormal ERG. Over 12 years her disease progressed dramatically, with marked loss of peripheral visual field. One daughter developed pattern macular dystrophy at age 31; at 44 her ERG was moderately abnormal but her disease was limited to the macula. The other daughter presented with macular degeneration at age 42 and over 10 years developed the picture of fundus flavimaculatus, with preserved peripheral field and a moderately abnormal ERG. The son had onset of macular degeneration at age 44, with pericentral scotomas, a markedly abnormal ERG and punctate pigment epithelial transmission defects on fluorescein angiography.
quotes: The mother presented at age 63 years with a profoundly abnormal electroretinogram (ERG) and adult-onset retinitis pigmentosa that progressed dramatically over 12 years, with marked loss of peripheral visual field.
One daughter developed pattern macular dystrophy at age 31 years. At age 44 years, her ERG was moderately abnormal but her clinical disease was limited to the macula.
Another daughter presented at age 42 years with macular degeneration and over 10 years developed the clinical picture of fundus flavimaculatus.

findings.statement: Weleber et al. (1993) found a new 3-bp deletion of codon 153 or 154 of the peripherin/RDS gene in a family whose members had retinitis pigmentosa, pattern macular dystrophy and fundus flavimaculatus. The authors concluded that this one mutation can produce clinically disparate phenotypes even within the same family.
quotes: We report herein the occurrence of three separate phenotypes within a single family with a novel 3-base pair deletion of codon 153 or 154 of the peripherin/RDS gene.
A 3-base pair deletion of codon 153 or 154 of the peripherin/RDS gene can produce clinically disparate phenotypes even within the same family.

findings.statement: Weleber et al. (1993) observed intrafamilial phenotypic variability: within a single family, the same peripherin/RDS codon 153/154 deletion caused retinitis pigmentosa, pattern macular dystrophy and fundus flavimaculatus.
quotes: A 3-base pair deletion of codon 153 or 154 of the peripherin/RDS gene can produce clinically disparate phenotypes even within the same family.

relevance_reason: This is the paper that first described digenic retinitis pigmentosa, with double heterozygosity for PRPH2 (peripherin/RDS) and ROM1 mutations. That is the subject of this entry.

findings.statement: Kajiwara et al. (1994) identified 3 families with mutations in the unlinked photoreceptor-specific genes ROM1 and peripherin/RDS. In these families, only individuals who were double heterozygotes, carrying a mutation in both genes, developed retinitis pigmentosa.
quotes: Three families were identified with mutations in the unlinked photoreceptor-specific genes ROM1 and peripherin/RDS, in which only double heterozygotes develop retinitis pigmentosa (RP).

findings.statement: Kajiwara et al. (1994) concluded that the allelic and nonallelic heterogeneity of monogenic retinitis pigmentosa is complicated further by interactions between unlinked mutations that cause digenic RP. They suggested that recognizing this inheritance pattern might help identify other examples of digenic inheritance in human disease.
quotes: These findings indicate that the allelic and nonallelic heterogeneity known to be a feature of monogenic RP is complicated further by interactions between unlinked mutations causing digenic RP.
Recognition of the inheritance pattern exemplified by these three families might facilitate the identification of other examples of digenic inheritance in human disease.

relevance_reason: The title reports a new peripherin/RDS (PRPH2) mutation, Asn244Lys, that causes autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa. This directly characterises RP7.

findings.statement: Kikawa et al. (1994) identified a novel mutation, Asn244Lys, in the peripherin/RDS gene causing autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa associated with bull's-eye maculopathy; the mutation was detected by nonradioisotopic SSCP analysis.
quotes: A novel mutation (Asn244Lys) in the peripherin/RDS gene causing autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa associated with bull's-eye maculopathy detected by nonradioisotopic SSCP.

relevance_reason: The paper linked late-onset autosomal dominant RP in an Irish pedigree to 6p, with no recombination at RDS. It named peripherin-RDS as a candidate gene, which is relevant to the mapping history of RP7.

findings.statement: Farrar et al. (1991) performed linkage analysis on an Irish pedigree with late-onset autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa using chromosome 6p markers. They found positive two-point lod scores with 5 markers, including D6S105 (Z = 6.081 at theta = 0.00), HLA-DRA (Z = 4.364 at theta = 0.00) and RDS (Z = 5.376 at theta = 0.00). Multipoint analysis gave a maximum lod score of 6.6 at HLA-DRA. The authors concluded that this localized the ADRP gene in the pedigree to 6p.
quotes: DNA from members of an Irish pedigree presenting with late onset autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (ADRP) have been typed with a series of genetic markers from chromosome 6p.
D6S105: theta = 0.00, Z = 6.081; HLA-DRA: theta = 0.00, Z = 4.364; and RDS: theta = 0.00, Z = 5.376
In a series of overlapping multipoint analyses a lod score of 6.6 was obtained, maximizing at HLA-DRA and hence localizing the ADRP gene (RP5) segregating in this pedigree to 6p.

findings.statement: Farrar et al. (1991) concluded that their findings were direct evidence for an additional autosomal dominant RP locus. They proposed the human equivalent of the mouse retinal degeneration slow (rds) gene, peripherin-RDS, as a strong candidate gene for autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa.
quotes: These data provide direct evidence for an additional autosomal dominant RP locus and strongly implicate the human equivalent of the mouse retinal degeneration slow (rds) gene, peripherin-rds, as a candidate for autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa.

relevance_reason: The paper reports a 3-bp deletion in peripherin/RDS that segregates with autosomal dominant RP in a large Irish pedigree linked to 6p, which is the founding molecular evidence for RP7.

findings.statement: In a large Irish pedigree with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa, Farrar et al. (1991) noted that the disease gene had been mapped to chromosome 6p and was tightly linked to the gene encoding peripherin, a photoreceptor cell-specific glycoprotein. This made peripherin a strong candidate gene.
quotes: A third adRP gene in a large Irish pedigree has been mapped to chromosome 6p, showing tight linkage with the gene for peripherin, a photoreceptor cell-specific glycoprotein, which is thus a strong candidate for the defective gene.

findings.statement: In affected members of a large Irish pedigree with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa linked to 6p, Farrar et al. (1991) identified a 3-bp deletion in the peripherin/RDS gene. The deletion removes one of a pair of highly conserved cysteine residues in the predicted third transmembrane domain of peripherin. It segregated with the disease and was not found in unaffected controls. The authors suggested that mutant peripherin causes retinitis pigmentosa.
quotes: We have now identified a three-base-pair deletion which results in the loss of one of a pair of highly conserved cysteine residues in the predicted third transmembrane domain of peripherin.
This deletion segregates with the disease phenotype but is not present in unaffected controls, and suggests that mutant peripherin gives rise to retinitis pigmentosa.

variants.as_reported: three-base-pair deletion resulting in loss of a conserved cysteine in the third transmembrane domain

relevance_reason: The paper reports that mutations in the human RDS (peripherin/RDS) gene cosegregate with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa, which defines RP7 at this locus.

findings.statement: Kajiwara et al. (1991) identified 3 mutations in RDS, the human homolog of the murine retinal degeneration slow (rds) gene, in separate families with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa. In each family the mutation cosegregated with the disease. The authors concluded that some cases of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa are due to mutations at the RDS locus.
quotes: We report here three mutations of the human homologue of the rds gene (RDS) that cosegregate with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa in separate families.
Our results indicate that some cases of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa are due to mutations at the RDS locus.

findings.statement: Kajiwara et al. (1991) noted that the murine retinal degeneration slow (rds) mutation is semidominant. In rds mice, rod and cone photoreceptors develop abnormally and then slowly degenerate, which made it a possible model for retinitis pigmentosa.
quotes: The murine retinal degeneration slow (rds) gene is a semidominant mutation with a phenotype having rod and cone photoreceptors that develop abnormally and then slowly degenerate.
The phenotype is a possible model for retinitis pigmentosa

relevance_reason: The paper reports linkage of a late-onset adRP locus on 6p to the peripherin-RDS gene in an Irish family. This is mapping evidence for RP7, which is the peripherin/RDS-associated form of RP.

findings.statement: In a large Irish family with late-onset autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa that had previously been linked to 6p, Jordan et al. (1992) found that an intragenic marker from the peripherin-RDS gene cosegregated with the disease locus with no recombination (lod score 5.46 at theta = 0.00).
quotes: an intrageneic marker derived from this gene cosegregated with the adRP disease locus with zero recombination (lod score 5.46 at q = .00)
localization of a gene for late-onset autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (adRP; RP6), on the short arm of chromosome 6, by linkage analysis in a large family of Irish origin

findings.statement: Jordan et al. (1992) used the CEPH reference panel to map the peripherin-RDS gene relative to other 6p markers. In a multipoint analysis, the lod score for adRP was 8.21 and peaked at the peripherin-RDS locus. The authors concluded that this was strong evidence suggesting a role for peripherin-RDS in the cause of one form of adRP.
quotes: Incorporation of these data into a multipoint analysis produced a lod score for adRP of 8.21, maximizing at the peripherin-RDS locus.
This study provides strong evidence suggesting a role for peripherin-RDS in the etiology of one form of adRP.
